newsitem.title: USA: Edelnor says Mejillones I problems solved.
newsitem.headline: Edelnor says Mejillones I problems solved.

text.p: Operating problems at Edelnor S.A.'s Mejillones I unit that resulted in sharply lower profits last year have been corrected, Chief Executive Officer Mark Lynch said on Monday.

Lynch said a drop in operations was primarily due to problems with control systems, which have been refigured by experts from 65 percent owner Southern Co. Edelnor completed the Mejillones I unit in January 1996.

"We can say, unequivocally, that we believe that the control and operation problems experienced in 1996 have been solved and we are looking forward to a much better year and meeting our performance expectations for 1997," Lynch said.
Edelnor reported a net profit of 0.12 billion pesos in 1996 versus 3.39 billion pesos in 1995. The 1996 results included a non-operating loss of 1.60 billion pesos.

The control reconfiguration was completed at the end of an outage in November and the unit has since been running at "expected" performance levels. In January, the unit ran at higher than 96 percent of capacity, he added.
A fall operations resulted in more purchased power at a higher marginal costs, Lynch said.
Lynch, Chief Financial Officer Jeff Spencer and Southern Energy CFO Ray Hill spoke to investors in a conference call sponsored by Salomon Brothers.

Lynch, who joined Edelnor in October, also said he initiated a downsizing of approximately 20 percent, effective at the end of February. The company hopes to realize in 1998 the effects of about $1.7 million per year.
Severance costs associated with the downsizing total $1.4 million to $1.5 million, he added.

Lynch said construction of the Mejillones II unit is expected to be completed by the end of March 1998. The Mejillones units are meant to allow Edelnor to replace costly purchased power and reduce exposure to spot prices.

In his opening remarks, Hill said Edelnor's financial results were also due to stiffer than anticipated competition in Chile's Northern Interconnected System (SING.) That problem is expected to persist into the future, although it was impossible to measure the degree going forward.

Lynch noted in its projections that Edelnor had misjudged the effects of competitive pressure on electric rates, which had already fallen to $38 per megawatt hour in 1995 from $60 per megawatt hour in 1993.
"That ($38) number we thought was very aggressive and that it was probably about the bottom of the market," Lynch said.
"As we went through 1996, though, we found that competition was doing what it was supposed to be doing in driving down costs and a large contract was signed at $35 per megawatt hour."
